newsitem.title: USA: FBI official sees long Democratic fund-raising probe.
newsitem.headline: FBI official sees long Democratic fund-raising probe.

text.p: A Justice Department task-force investigation into Democratic campaign fund raising may be lengthy as investigators review records and then question individuals, an FBI official said Friday.

Thomas Pickard, who recently became assistant director in charge of the FBI's office in Washington, D.C., doubted that investigators will "get to the bottom of it very quickly," although he was unable to predict how long it might take.

He told reporters that investigators first need to review the fund-raising records and then would have to conduct interviews, asking people about the records. Investigators need to gain cooperation from individuals involved, he said.
Under pressure from Republicans in Congress, the Justice Department last year set up a task force to investigate questionable Democratic campaign fund raising, mainly involving foreign sources.
The probe seeks to determine whether Clinton administration or Democratic National Committee officials violated any criminal laws in fund-raising activities stemming from the 1996 elections.

FBI Director Louis Freeh said in a letter to Congress this week that 25 agents had been assigned to the task force. He vowed to provide "whatever additional resources and support are needed as the investigation develops."
Many of the agents assigned to the task force come from the FBI's Washington field office, which falls under Pickard's jurisdiction.
In a get-acquainted session with reporters, Pickard said he did not know how long it would take to review the fund-raising records, adding that it would depend on their "volume and complexity."
But he acknowledged that investigations involving "voluminous records," such as the Whitewater probe of President Clinton's real estate investment in Arkansas while he was governor, often last years.
Pickard said the fund-raising probe keeps expanding "everytime I read the newspapers." The investigation last month was broadened to cover questionable contributions to Clinton's legal defence fund.

Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick Thursday declined comment on whether the task force would examine the controversial coffee sessions at the White House that the Democratic National Committee set up and Clinton attended.
